title: How Russia Is Attacking the Midterms with a Mother Jones Deepfake

reading.body:
This is an impersonation failure at the point of publication. A fabricated video carried the branding of a news outlet and a fabricated endorsement from that outlet's editor, and it was distributed on a social platform where it accumulated views before any correction. The false claim at its centre, that a political party paid a broadcaster's executive to promote gender transition in children, was presented as reported fact rather than as opinion or satire.

The failure sits in the platform's distribution layer rather than in any model's output. The video was removed only after the impersonated outlet complained, and the stated ground for removal was trademark, not the falsity of the claim. Catching this earlier would have required either automated detection of forged outlet branding at upload or a takedown path keyed to the falsity of the content rather than to the rights of the brand being copied. Neither is shown to have existed here.

What is not established is who produced the video, whether any named individual directed it, and whether the campaign changed any viewer's beliefs or behaviour. The attribution to a named network comes from researchers and a tracking group, not from a court or an official finding.

reports.title: How Russia Is Attacking the Midterms with a Mother Jones Deepfake

summary:
A Russian disinformation network known as Storm-1679 or Matryoshka has been spreading fake videos on US social media ahead of the 2026 midterms. One video, falsely branded with a Mother Jones logo, claimed the Democratic National Committee paid $259 million to CNN chief Mark Thompson to promote gender transition among children, and it falsely showed Mother Jones editor-in-chief Clara Jeffery praising the story. It drew 155,000 views on one X account and 50,000 on another within a day. The campaign also used deepfakes of celebrities such as Sarah Jessica Parker and Julia Roberts, plus fake reports impersonating major outlets like CNN, the New York Times, and NPR.

The operation was first spotted by the anonymous tracking group @antibot4navalny. After Mother Jones complained, X removed the fake video for violating its trademark policy. Researchers say the campaign has not yet gained major reach, though a similar 2024 effort spread false claims about Kamala Harris and Tim Walz to millions. The article notes that the Trump administration has closed FBI, intelligence, and State Department units that once tracked Russian disinformation, leaving the US less able to counter such operations before the midterms.
